papers.title: ShadowScope: From GPU Kernel Validation to Governing AI Chip Usage
papers.abstract: Modern AI accelerators such as GPUs support a wide range of workloads, from scientific computing to deep learning training. As AI regulation and export controls increase, there is a growing need to verify what types of computations are performed on regulated hardware. In this paper, we present ShadowScope, a system that uses GPU hardware performance counters (accessed via CUPTI PMU) to validate GPU kernel behavior. We demonstrate that performance counter signatures can distinguish between different kernel types and detect attempts to disguise ML training workloads. Our approach provides a foundation for hardware-based compute governance mechanisms.
papers.tldr: Uses GPU hardware performance counters via CUPTI PMU to validate GPU kernel behavior and distinguish ML training from other workloads.
papers.notes: Core reference for this SPAR project. Directly addresses our research question.

papers.title: Rendered Insecure: GPU Side Channel Attacks are Practical
papers.abstract: Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) are commonly integrated in modern computing platforms and are being increasingly used to accelerate computation in many domains beyond graphics rendering. This paper demonstrates practical GPU side-channel attacks. We present three attacks that exploit GPU performance counters and contention on GPU resources. Our attacks work across different GPU applications and in cross-process scenarios, demonstrating information leakage about GPU computations from colocated processes.
papers.tldr: Demonstrates practical GPU side-channel attacks exploiting performance counters and resource contention to leak information about GPU computations.

papers.title: Secure, Governable Chips: Using On-Chip Mechanisms to Manage National Security Risks from AI & Advanced Computing
papers.abstract: This report examines how on-chip governance mechanisms could help manage national security risks from advanced AI systems. As AI capabilities advance and concerns about misuse grow, policymakers need technical tools to enforce compute governance. We propose a framework of hardware-level mechanisms including secure boot, remote attestation, and usage logging that could be implemented in future AI accelerator chips. These mechanisms would enable verification of how regulated chips are being used without requiring trust in the end user.
papers.tldr: Proposes on-chip governance mechanisms including secure boot, remote attestation, and usage logging for AI accelerator chips to enable compute governance.
papers.notes: CNAS policy report. Key reference for governance motivation.

papers.title: Hardware-Enabled Governance Mechanisms: Developing Technical Solutions to Manage AI Chip Access
papers.abstract: As AI hardware becomes increasingly central to national security, there is a growing need for technical mechanisms to govern access to and use of AI chips. This report explores hardware-enabled governance mechanisms that can be implemented in current and future AI accelerators. We examine approaches including firmware-based usage controls, cryptographic attestation, and hardware performance monitoring for verifying chip usage patterns. Our analysis considers the trade-offs between governance capability and performance overhead, and provides recommendations for policymakers and chip manufacturers.
papers.tldr: Explores hardware-enabled governance mechanisms for AI chips, including firmware controls, cryptographic attestation, and performance monitoring.
papers.notes: RAND report on hardware governance mechanisms.

papers.title: Forecasting GPU Performance for Deep Learning Training and Inference
papers.abstract: Understanding and predicting GPU performance for deep learning workloads is critical for efficient resource allocation and hardware design. This paper presents a performance forecasting framework that decomposes deep learning workloads into constituent kernel types (GEMM, convolution, element-wise, reduction, etc.) and models their behavior on GPU hardware. We demonstrate that workload decomposition into kernel types provides accurate performance predictions across different GPU architectures and DL models. Our analysis reveals distinctive patterns in how different DL workloads utilize GPU resources.
papers.tldr: Decomposes deep learning workloads into GPU kernel types (GEMM, convolution, etc.) to forecast performance, revealing distinctive resource utilization patterns.
papers.notes: ASPLOS 2025. Useful for understanding ML training kernel signatures.
